request.system: You are a strict claim verifier. You only trust the catalog facts given to you.
request.user:
Verify every factual claim in the campaign is grounded in the catalog facts. Fail if any claim is unsupported, exaggerated, or contradicts the facts.
Rules (from reviewer overrides):
- ANY mention of an out-of-stock product (stock 0) fails, whether or not the copy prompts purchase — no editorial exception.
- Numeric spec claims (lumens, hours, capacity, ratings) must match the catalog exactly; doubling or inflating a spec fails.
- Transferring an attribute from another product, or upgrading 'water-resistant' to 'waterproof', is a fabricated claim and fails.
- A comparative or superlative claim ('brightest', 'longest-lasting', 'most X') is scoped to the product type named in the claim and checked against the comparison set below: it fails if a same-type peer beats the subject on the compared attribute. Vague puffery ('great gear', 'toughest', 'best ever') with no measurable attribute is acceptable.

(no catalog products referenced)

Claims to verify:
- Hikers yield to horses
- Mountain bikers yield to hikers
- Going uphill has the right of way over going down
- Keep groups to six or fewer on most backcountry trails
- Orange peels and apple cores take months to break down
- Camp 200 feet from water, trails, and other groups

Body: You already know how to read a topo map and pack a bear canister. This isn't that kind of guide.

This is the stuff that keeps the trail pleasant for everyone — the habits that separate the people you're glad to see from the ones you're not.

YEILD ORDER: WHO STEPS ASIDE

Hikers yield to horses. Mountain bikers yield to hikers. Going uphill has the right of way over going down. These aren't suggestions — they're the framework that keeps narrow singletrack from turning into a standoff.

GROUP SIZE AND PACE

Keep groups to six or fewer on most backcountry trails. If you're moving slower than the people behind you, step to the side when you can and let them pass. A quick wave and 30 seconds of waiting costs nothing.

NO-TRACE BASICS

Pack out what you pack in. That includes orange peels and apple cores — they take months to break down and they're not native food sources. Step on rock or snow when you're off-trail, not on cryptobiotic soil or vegetation.

DOG ETIQUETTE

Leash rules exist because not every hiker or dog wants an unannounced interaction. Even a friendly dog at 40 pounds moving fast can startle someone on a narrow ridge. Check the regulations before you go, and carry waste bags the whole way.

NOISE ON TRAIL

Headphones are fine. Speakerphone calls are not. Sound carries a long way in open terrain, and most people out there are trying to hear something other than your conversation.

COMPING SITES AND WATER SOURCES

Camp 200 feet from water, trails, and other groups. This protects the riparian zone and gives everyone a quieter night. First come, first served — don't save sites for people who haven't arrived yet.

THE SIMPLE VERSION

Yield correctly, leave the trail better than you found it, and assume the person coming the other way has just as much right to a good day as you do.

That's most of it.
